“HKS,” Mydei scoffs, “she would have beheaded you for your words before you would even get the chance.”

Phainon laughs and looks over. “I guess you’re right! I’m an insensitive bastard, right? Ah, Mydeimos, you break my heart. They look like they’re having fun though. I wonder what they’re celebrating?”

“Maybe they’re celebrating Era Nova!”

Phainon smiles wistfully. “Yes, maybe,” he agrees quietly. “Maybe Era Nova’s come for them.”

Something’s wrong, Mydei thinks, but he’s not sure what it is. Something’s wrong with what Phainon’s saying. But what is it? What is he missing? It feels so small, so insignificant, and yet it is so momentous. Just thinking about it leaves him bereft of breath.

I have gazed you, the voice returns, and in turn, you have gazed me. Continue on, o hallowed child of Amphoreus.

There’s rumbling again and they worry once more about the roof caving in, but nothing of the sort happens. Instead, on the far side of the room, a new doorway appears, because that’s not creepy whatsoever.

“Sure,” Phainon says nonchalantly, “that’s normal. That’s just how doors work. Appearing out of nowhere. Anyway, I vote we go. What’s the worst that could happen?”

“We could die,” Mydei responds instantly.

Phainon sighs deep. “It was a rhetoric question, Mydeimos. Can you haul your conspicuous body over there, please?”

“I can, yes.”

“That was—you know what, forget it. I’ll go first. Duck, duck, go!”

Mydei frowns. What’s that supposed to mean? Is there a duck? Is he supposed to duck? He’d like to see the duck, if there is one. As they leave, Mydei throws one last glance back at the mirror—maybe just to make sure he didn’t make all of this up. And sure enough, the mirror still stands, but he thinks—he thinks he sees a faint crack, but he is left with no time to dwell on it, as Phainon marches ever forward.

“There are more symbols now,” Tribbie remarks as she holds the torch high. He’s surprised it hasn’t burned out yet, but he’s grateful. He’s no stranger to

fighting in the dark, and he knows Phainon is more than capable himself, but protecting Tribios might be too difficult in the dark.

“Yes,” Phainon agrees, “but they seem to be getting all over the place; more like mad scribbles. Should I take pictures of them, too?”

“Sure! The more, the merrier, right? Maybe Naxy can analyse them too? He’d be sure to figure out what they mean, right, Snowy?”

Phainon hums only in agreement as he lifts his teleslate again, waiting for Tribbie to get into position. Mydei steps up next to him, looking at the screen.

“I do not like this place,” he states, “we should attempt to leave as soon as possible.”

“Yeah,” Phainon nods, “but if you can’t punch the wall down, we have little choice but to continue with whatever is going on. At least it’s not been malevolent so far, right? I thought about smashing the mirror, but what if the whole thing collapses on us then? We don’t even know how far we are underground. If only there were a window somewhere... we could even climb up by the side of a cliff.”

Mydei hums. He’s of the same mind, and hopefully Zagreus will be on their side. Even a temple underground would beget a window or two, right? He still doesn’t understand how in the world the door just fucking disappeared. Doors don’t do that. They also don’t just appear randomly on previously barren walls. They shouldn’t have investigated, they should’ve fucking blown the place up and call it a day.

He grabs Phainon’s hand on instinct alone. The man jumps a little, clearly surprised, and he turns to Mydei with big question marks in his eyes. He hasn’t checked the bandages in a few days, but he knows they’re there.

“Stay close to me,” he commands, “no matter what happens.”

Phainon blinks, taken aback, and then he smiles softly.

“Of course,” he promises, “I’ll always be right behind you, Mydei.”

Satisfied, Mydei nods. He gives Phainon’s hand one last squeeze before he lets go again. Part of him wants to ask if his wounds hurt, but the more rational part of him tells him it’s fruitless to ask.

“We see another door! Come on you two, let’s hurry! Tribbie misses the sun~”

“Coming, coming,” Phainon laughs, putting his teleslate away before quickly following their little guide. Mydei watches his back for a moment, before he, too, follows.

The next room looks much like the first, just a little smaller. Here, again, stands a mirror, larger than him.

I now pose a question upon thee, the voice from the walls whispers, hollow child, what have your golden eyes spied? Answer me, and make your way unto the future.

Mydei frowns. Out of the three of them, he’s the only one that could be considered having golden eyes, but somehow, he doesn’t feel like he’s been addressed at all. Did the voice expect somehow else? He exchanges a glance with Phainon, and the Deliverer clenches his jaw.

“I’ll go first,” he says then, “it’s only fair, right?”

Mydei crosses his arms and nods. He wants to fidget, and he doesn’t fidget. He can’t even blame this sudden want onto Phainon. He looks around, but there’s nothing there. No monster, no nothing, not even any destroyed structures. This place feels artificial. Like it exists for one and one purpose only, but what? These mirrors... what do they really mean? Why did all see what they did? And what could they possibly see now?

Phainon steps before the mirror and he tilts his head a bit, stepping closer still, as if he couldn’t see anything within. He pulls a face and squints, rubbing his palm over the surface. Mydei frowns. Isn’t he seeing anything? Or is he going blind? With Phainon, you never really know. Then, however,

the Deliverer freezes and suddenly goes very, very rigid. He presses his hand against the mirror, eyes wide and mouth agape, shaking his head minutely.

“Deliverer—“ Mydei starts but never gets to finish. Black fog emerges from the mirror, quickly followed by the loud bang of an explosion, and Mydei’s world goes dark. He doesn’t even see what’s happened to Phainon or Tribbie. He hopes they’re alright. He hopes they didn’t get hurt.

When he comes back to, he has no idea how much time has passed. Groaning, he turns his head to the side, dizzy and blurry in eyesight, and he thinks he sees Tribbie lie next to him. She can’t be dead... right? No. No, she’s just—knocked out. He forces himself to turn and he almost has to puke, but he suppresses the urge. He reaches out and gently shakes her small body and she whimpers slightly, unwaking. He breathes out. Good. She’s still alive. He blinks and restrains himself from shaking his head and he looks around. Phainon is like a beacon in the dark, but he can’t see him anywhere. And there’s... not enough rubble for him to be buried. Mydei closes his eyes and instead strains his hearing. Yes; he can make out the distant sound of fighting. Chances are; he’ll find Phainon there. But... he can’t leave Tribbie here all alone. What if someone finds her while she’s helpless?

Groaning, he gathers her in his arms and pushes himself upwards. The world swims before his eyes and he figures he must’ve gained a concussion. Just what had happened? No matter, he can try to find out later. Right now, Phainon will need his assistance.

He progresses slower than he would wish for. His vision swims, and he has difficulty walking in a straight line. He can pull through, though; he’s a warrior of Castrum Kremnos. What would his people say if they saw him defeated by a measly concussion?

The noise is getting louder now. He has to be close. And sure enough, when he turns a corner—had there been one before?—he sees Phainon in all his glory, battling against the creatures of the black tide and titankin alike. He... wants to help. But instead of taking a step forward, he falls to his knees

again. This shouldn’t happen. He should... he should be fine. He’s Mydeimos the Undying, he shouldn’t...

“Deliverer,” he shouts as loud as he can, barely a whisper against his tongue, but the Deliverer turns still and his eyes widen but before Mydei can think more of it, darkness’ veil puts itself over him. How odd, he thinks, he can’t remember closing his eyes.

Tell me, o void child, what hast thou seen in mirrors hence?

A memory you could lose yourself in: everyone he knows and loves, safe and sound in a home that is no longer, with golden fields softly swaying in the ever-gentle wind. If he tries just hard enough, he can hear them laugh, too. They will never turn around to look at him; because for their happiness, he cannot exist.

A future where you have lost yourself: he saw himself staring back, unmoving, cold and cracked at the very core, and worst of all, clad in that damned black that has haunted his mind for years now. Sunken eyes, devoid of any life and the very tip of that sword dipped in dried golden blood. The blazing sun, enthralled in thorns, bleeding golden blood and under its weight, he still could never crumble.

And after that…

The swordsman looked straight at him and came out of the mirror, ready to take Phainon away. He blacked out then, and when he woke up, he could feel a blaring pain in his leg. He hisses at it and looks down, finding an arrow lodged straight into his thigh. Turning his head, he finds both Mydei and Tribbie lie on the floor unmoving and he makes his way over to them to try and wake them. Tribbie has a wound on her temple, and she’s likely concussed but she still lives. That has to be good enough for now, and

Mydei…Mydei seems unharmed, but he, too, is knocked out cold. Who knew that there is a word for blacking out in the Kremnoan language? Phainon lets out a hefty breath and looks at his own leg again. They didn’t bring any bandages with them—Mydei not ever needing them, and Phainon usually agile enough to avoid having to need them. It would probably the better idea to leave the arrow in, so that he wouldn’t bleed out. Should he break the shaft off? But what if the arrowhead would slip in further then? Hyacine is going to kill him… ugh, hopefully he can deal with this on his own before they get back to Okhema so he wouldn’t even have to tell her.

He hears sounds and his blood runs cold.

Panicked, he looks around, standing up. Sudden sounds are always bad. After having encountered nothing, sudden sounds can only mean monsters. He summons his sword and looks around. He can’t fight here. He absolutely cannot risk Tribbie and Mydei to get out hurt while they’re down. He tightens his grip and runs towards the origin of the sound, hoping to intercept them before they can get here.

Mydei just needs to wake up, and then it’ll be all fine. Phainon can hold out until then.

Phainon runs down yet another cursed corridor and he sharply turns a corner, where he finds the sound’s origins. Titankin, and worse still, black tide monsters mixed in with them. Usually they don’t mingle, but this place is weird enough that it hardly surprises him. No matter. He just has to push them back here, and all will be fine. It’s not like these monsters are endless, right? Everything ends.

He slices the first enemy clean in half and he runs further into the room. He wants them to focus on the opposite site from where he came from—once Mydei gets here, he doesn’t need the man ambushed straight away.

Phainon dodges the next two attacks, and blocks the third. He has to be careful with the black tide. Chrysos Heirs are naturally more resistant to its effects, but they’re hardly immune to it. As long as he can avoid open wounds and their weapons lodged into him, he should be fine. He evades an arrow in the last moment and decides it would probably be wise to deal

with the backline first. He body-slams into an enemy to shove them aside and he breaks through, rolling over the ground to hopefully make two enemies hit each other and with one swing he cuts the archer’s legs off, before he rams his blade in their chest, hopefully eliminating them for good.

Sensing something approach from behind, he jumps to the side, locking his eyes on the next archer. There are four here, but as long as he can get rid of at least two; he should be in a better position. One enemy punches him in the leg and Phainon grunts, jumping forwards and swinging his sword before looking. The head makes a hard sound upon hitting the ground, much like a stone upon marble. Then, he rolls out of dodge and gets upright again. He must take note of the wall, because he doesn’t want to get backed into a corner.

He quickly evades some of the Warrior’s swings and when they bend over, having tried to grab him, he jumps up and uses their back to launch himself into the air, coming down again with a powerful blow, killing two creatures of the black tide. He’s doing well, but there are still so many enemies. At least none of them are focused on the corridor he came out of. His mind keeps drifting off though, and he forces it to remain on track. He can lose himself later.

I see Hephaestion and the others.

No. He can’t think about that now. With any luck, whatever he’s feeling about that will be gone by the time they make it out of here. Speaking of, how are they going to do that? Well, the monster had to come from somewhere, right? Maybe that blasted mirror could be useful for once.

Phainon moves to block two attacks at once and oddly, his legs are growing tired. That shouldn’t happen so soon. He’s been fighting for long enough that his body got used to the strain and as much as he enjoys complaining to Mydei about his soreness, he isn’t actually that frail. He grits his teeth and decides to ignore it. Whatever it is, he can deal with this later. Where the fuck is Mydei? The man does not need additional beauty sleep. Phainon wishes he were only a third as pretty as Mydeimos.

“Deliverer—“ he finally hears, but as he turns his head, maybe to chastise Mydei for taking so long, his eyes widen instead. Mydei has come out of the corridor and he’s holding Tribbie in his arm, but—can’t he see? Doesn’t he know? Right next to him stands a monster with its greatsword raised high and before Phainon can shout out a warning, anything at all—the blade goes down, and Mydei’s head makes a soft sound on the ground, like a pomegranate splitting on the dirt.

The sound of his body follows, a dull thud, and golden blood spills on the ground and Phainon is frozen in shock because—because—because—

He’s dreaming. It’s the mirror. It’s something, because—because—because —because Mydei can’t be dead. No. He refuses it to be true. It’s a trick of the light. An illusion of the darkness. Something. Anything. He doesn’t care.

He gets forced out of his reverie by a blade piercing his middle and in the blind hot pain he remembers he’s still on a battlefield. He growls and whips himself around, cleaving the head off his assailant’s shoulders in one fell swoop. He needs to get to Mydei and Tribbie. They’re vulnerable, and he won’t let them fall. So he sprints over to them as fast as his worryingly quick numb growing legs allow and he cuts the titankin with the greatsword in half. He whips around and blocks an enemy sword with his bracer while stabbing something else through the face. He has no more time for dilly-dallying. He grips his sword with both hands and swings it in a wide cleave, taking several monsters out. His middle grows sickeningly wet and heavy, but he’s no time to think about that. One after another, they fall before him.

His sword shatters before the fight ends, and he curses the shoddy blade work. He’s shattered every gods-forsaken sword he’s been given, and now it decides it’s time? Whatever. Phainon is far from helpless and with a roar, he grabs the monster before him and tosses it into its friends. He dodge-rolls to the side and picks up the fallen greatsword. It’s far bigger than what he’s used to, but when did that ever stop him? The sword burns the palms of his hands and with a shout; he throws himself forward, driving the corrupted blade through a titankin. Using the momentum, he turns and raises the blade upward, straight into a black tide creature trying to ambush him from

above. He flips over an enemy to land again on his feet, swinging his blade around him.

His feet slip on the blood on the ground, but he adjusts his stance and jumps up, kneeing something in the face and not feeling the impact it should have and then he twirls around, cutting a few heads in half during the movement.

His breaths come heavy when the last monster falls and Phainon’s eyes scan the battlefield, just in case he’s missed something. But nothing is moving. He’s... won. His gaze finds Mydei and Tribbie again and he knows he still has no time to breathe.

The blade clutters to the ground and he rushes over to them. He skitters on the ground and heaves Mydei’s body around, to check for Tribbie’s life-signs. She doesn’t move, and her head is wounded, but she still breathes. For now, that has to be enough. A part of him had hoped that maybe he could waste more time on her, so he wouldn’t have to face the ugly truth, but perhaps it’s best done while adrenaline still cruises through his veins. So he turns to Mydei and he pushes his body straight and after a moment, pulls it away from the golden blood crowning it. Crowned in blood, and he won’t, he won’t. Not even trying to control his breathing, he looks towards —towards Mydei’s head. His hands shake when he crawls over to reach for it and titans, he’s lucky nothing’s happened to it during the fight. He picks it up gently and Mydei’s eyes are still half-open. Choking on the bile in his throat, Phainon closes the golden eyes and turns back to the headless body before him. He doesn’t even try to stand up, and instead robs his way there on his knees. His legs are—numb, even more, but he has no time to think about it.

Maybe the easiest solution will work. Mydei’s body is unstudied territory, after all. So he just—holds the head back on the stump, hoping it’ll just... grow back on, or something, but of course, he’s no such luck.  Phainon doesn’t even know if Mydei’s ever lost limbs before and if he did, how he worked around that. Do they re-grow when he returns to life? But surely, there’s a difference between an arm and a head, no?

No matter what, he’s not going to test it. What if Mydei would come back to life just to die again immediately? No. No, he needs to... re-attach the

head... yeah, that’s easy. Why is Hyacine not here? Hyacine should be here. He can’t heal. He can’t care for anything. He can’t even care for himself, for crying out loud!

His breaths become sporadic and he notices; and he needs to calm down. He can’t get a panic attack now, because if he gets one now, they’re all doomed. He presses his eyes shut and bends over, hugging Mydei’s head close to his middle. Fuck, he’s still bleeding himself, but what difference does a little blood make in the grand scheme of things?

“Okay,” he breathes and sits up straight again, “okay.”

He looks around. How do you re-attach anything? Stitches, probably. But he doesn’t have any, so he’ll have to improvise. Firstly, he needs to make sure to fasten the head to the neck somewhat securely. But with what? He has nothing. Wait. His leatherband. Maybe he can use that as a base? He gently puts the head back on the ground and unfastens the band, looking at it. It’s never ripped on him before, even when he’s had to strain his neck, and he and Mydei have a similar build, so it’ll fit for sure. But that only won’t be enough, so what else is there? Even if he were able to rip his clothes for strings, he has no needle, and not even anything close to it. Is there something here he can use? Surely it’s not too much to ask that one of the titankin carry a sewing kit? Fruitless, of course, but... their bodies are hard, aren’t they? He crawls over to the closest felled enemy and inspects its body. It looks a little bit like crystal, doesn’t it? It’s hard enough for sure. If he could chip some parts off... he looks to where he’s dropped the sword and immediately decides against it; that blade is way too large. But his own hands would be too soft; and if he breaks his hand now, that would spell disastrous. He looks to Mydei. Mydei’s gauntlets would be hard enough. He doesn’t need to feel them, they just need to work.

He gently unclasps the gauntlet and slides it onto his own arm. It feels odd, if he’s honest. He’s never worn them before; never even wanted to, but there’s a first time for everything. He hobbles back over to the titankin and starts punching its arm until splinters are starting to fall off. He tears the

arm a little, trying to break off fragments that are long enough. He tries to bend one, just to see if they can, but it breaks between his fingers. No good, then. Fair enough.

He continues until he has seven pieces of roughly the same length, and they just have to be enough. He hurries back over to Mydei and now he hesitates. How does he do this? He’s afraid the band and the splinters won’t be enough on their own. Think. Think, Phainon! You’re no debate champion for nothing.

Hold on, his cape! He can use that! Can’t he? Aglaea will surely forgive him. He unfastens the cape and thinks—band or cape first? No, band. He doesn’t want to get the cloth inside of Mydei be accident, or something. If only Tribbie were awake, then she could just whisk them back away to Okhema. He hauls Mydei’s body next to a low wall and carefully manoeuvres him into a position where he won’t slide down. Okay. Great. Hurriedly, Phainon goes to retrieve the head and carefully, ever so carefully, places it back on the neck, and then holds it tight with all his might—and one hand. Quickly, he wraps the band around Mydei’s neck—it’s a little hard to fasten it with just one hand, but he makes do. He pulls it a little tighter than he would on himself, but it’s alright, isn’t it? Okay, okay. He’s breathing too quickly again, but he has no time to think about regulating it. He can breathe when he’s dead, really. Phainon swallows around the bile in his throat and reaches over to grab the carefully collected splinters, still holding Mydeimos’ head tight.

“Sorry,” he breathes as he pushes the fragments through skin and flesh. He still has one gauntlet on, but he barely notices. His vision blurs at times, but he pushes through until all the splinters are in place. It’s not pretty, and he doubts it’s functional, but he has nothing else. His hope of Tribbie waking up dwindles with every passing moment, but he can’t give up. Okay. Okay. He gently lowers Mydei back down onto the floor and pulls his cape close. He should probably try to wrap Mydei’s head completely, and then try to tie it back to his body, right? At least his cape isn’t made of flimsy material,

thank Aglaea. He carefully rips it into several strips, and then starts wrapping it around Mydei’s head. A couple times around the head, then a couple times around the neck and he has just enough left to wrap it once around his chest. It’s a tight fit, but if it works, it works. Okay. Now, he needs to... test it. He closes his eyes and breathes a couple times. He can do this. It’ll be fine. He grabs Mydei’s shoulders and gently pulls him up, keeping his eyes shut. He’s waiting to hear the same sound again, and when no such thing happens, he blinks one eye open to peek at Mydei’s head still being attached. Oh... oh, thank fuck. Okay. Okay, that’s good. Not wanting to push his luck, he lowers Mydei back down again and crawls over to Tribbie, shaking her a little. Her head wound looks nasty, but it’s stopped bleeding.

“Lady Tribbie,” he calls, “please wake up. Please. I need your help.”

Of course, he’s not so lucky, and besides her quiet breathing, there’s no sign she’s even still alive. Fuck it. He sits back on his hunches and looks around. He needs to get out of here. He needs to get back to Okhema. With his luck, the dromas ran off too. But how does he get out of here? Sighing, he stands up on numb legs and he looks over to the far wall. If he’s not wrong, this might be an outer wall, and with that, his only chance. He balls his fist still in Mydei’s gauntlet, and he walks over full of determination. He stops before the wall and he breathes in deep, trying to calm his troubled mind. He fails, and he punches the wall as hard as he can. The reverberations travel up his arm into his head, but he grits his teeth and he tries again and again and again until the wall crumbles under his blow.  Phainon almost stumbles and falls outside, but he steadies himself the last minute. He can see...

He can see the sky. However, there is no ground for him to step on. He looks down a sharp Cliffside, until he spies the ocean below. Great. He leans forward a little and looks up the raggedy site and wonders how far down they are. At least he can see the sky, so that’s got to count for something, right?

Phainon doesn’t have a choice; he’ll need to climb up. He goes back inside and stares at Mydei and Tribbie lying on the ground. How is he going to transport them? He can’t hold them if he needs his hands to climb. Hmm.

Oh! What about his coat? It should be long enough, right? He’ll put Mydei on his back, and try to strap Tribbie to his chest. He hurries back to them and strips himself. Well, this has to work, because after this, he’ll have nothing else. He pulls Mydei on his back and he hunches over, trying to wrap the coat around him enough to ensure he doesn’t drop. So, under his buttocks and around his middle... okay... and then Tribbie too, shoving her into his chest and tying the cloth tight. He does some experimental little jumps, but neither of them falls out. Hopefully the climb won’t be that long.

Phainon closes his eyes and walks back to the hole. It’ll be fine. If he goes slowly, it’ll be fine. The wind is cold and harsh in his face, and he breathes in deep. No use in dilly-dallying. If Tribbie showed signs of waking up, then maybe, but she’s as still as a stone. At least she’s breathing, so that’s something. Mydei is cold and heavy on his back, but that’s okay.

“Let’s go,” he hypes himself up, “golden boy of Okhema, Deliverer of Era Nova, let’s go.”

He’s still wearing Mydei’s gauntlet. Well, maybe it’ll help find crevices while he climbs. He swallows down hard and decides he’s stalled long enough. He places his hands on the rocks and then swings his legs out. It’s difficult; to climb with numb legs, but he’ll make do. His arms are stringer anyway, so he’ll rely on them. Mydei never says nice things about his arms, it’s always just thighs, thighs and more thighs. Personally, he thinks they could use some more muscle, but he hasn’t had time to come up with a new training regime.

It’s awkward, having to watch out for Tribbie’s head. He won’t slam her against the rocks, so he needs to ascend while a little hunched. At least Mydei stays somewhat secured, even though Phainon can feel that he’s slipping a little.

His arms burn from the sting and it really was a great idea to cut himself nearly to the bone just before they departed. Truly, he’s the king of timings. Whatever. So he bleeds a little more, what’s the big deal? At least his hands stay blood-free and he only has to worry about sweat.

“Mydei,” he pants half-way up the Cliffside, “please help me. You always help me.”

But Mydei stays silent. Phainon closes his eyes, longing for a break, and pulls himself up further. He’s not going to give up, even if his arms fall off. His feet keep losing ground, but that’s okay, because his arms are working double-time.

It feels like forever until he’s able to pull himself over the edge and he crawls away from the cliff, allowing himself to collapse to the side for a minute. He’s dizzy, his vision swims and he can’t breathe properly. But he’s made it. He’s made it to the top, and neither Tribbie nor Mydei were lost in the process.

Phainon desperately wants to close his eyes and sleep, but he can’t. What if there are monsters about? Besides, he needs to get back to Okhema to report to Aglaea. So, he heaves out a breath and pushes himself up again. Standing on shaking legs, he re-adjusts both Mydei and Tribbie to make sure they’re staying secure. He hooks his arms under Mydei’s legs for added security and hopes Tribbie’s sling will hold. But... which direction is Okhema? He’s usually good with directions. Maybe he should just aim to find a road first. If he’s lucky, he’ll find a caravan heading to the Holy City as well and they could hitch-hike. Or Tribbie would wake up and contact Trinnon and Trianne... or did the two already realise that Tribbie isn’t asleep?

“Heave-ho,” he whispers, “duck, duck, go.”

He’s no idea how long he’s been walking for, He’s still bleeding, he thinks, but he’s not sure. He’s pretty sure that that arrow had been poisoned—he can’t explain the persisting numbness otherwise. And the gash in his middle... he doesn’t want to think about the sickening feeling within. If he doesn’t think about it, then it’ll go away, right? And at least his left arm is bleeding. He’s not sure about the right, because the gauntlet might be too taut. Whatever. He shouldn’t think about that.

I see Hephaestion and the others.

Stupid. Stupid, stupid, stupid. What reason is there to be jealous of a dead man? And yet, he can’t help but be insecure: if Hephaestion had made it into Okhema with Mydei, then—would Mydei have spared him any thought at all? In his dreams, the Kremnoan sometimes calls for his old friends. It’s fine. Phainon’s sure he’s called for Cyrene at some point, too, but... it’s different, isn’t it? Mydei isn’t as insecure as he is.

Mydei had seemed guilty when he’d looked away from the mirror. Why? Had he secretly lavished in a fantasy that Phainon didn’t exist in? It’s alright. It’s gotta be alright. Phainon already knows that he can’t stand next to Mydei in any other context but combat. And Krateros, the closest thing Mydei has to a mentor, can’t stand him... what if that old man compares Phainon to Hephaestion and finds him lacking? After all, according to Mydei, Hephaestion had been a sight to behold on the battlefield.

You don’t truly love combat.

Phainon’s leg buckle, but he catches himself before he falls. His insides throb in pain and misery, but he has to keep moving. Forward, ever forward. He can’t fall, he can’t give up; the things he carries are far too important.

May this world never again need a Deliverer.

He grits his teeth and his ankle rolls on a loose rock on the path and he stumbles, landing hard on his knee. He just catches himself on one hand, curling his fingers in the dirt before he pushes through and stands back up again.

He tries, doesn’t he? He tries so hard, he just wishes it were enough. He will never hold it against Aglaea, but it took her three months to even ask his name. Trianne had told him of this Cifera and he didn’t know why, but it had stung somewhere—still does, on bad days. Tribbie has told him how much Aglaea cared about this Cifera, just akin to a daughter really, and he remembers thinking that it surely hadn’t taken her three months to ask Cifera’s name. He’d never say it out loud, but he knows he’s just a rebound.

That’s all he ever is, isn’t he? He can just hope that in the end, at least someone remembers him in the margin of their own stories.

Hephaestion braided it for me.

What is he going to leave behind? His inability to save money; up to a point where Aglaea is keeping track of his spending? The alleged atrocious way he’d dress himself, if Aglaea hadn’t colour-coordinated his entire wardrobe? Mydei, he thinks, you’ll meet so many great warriors, why would you ever remember our spars? I’m just a placeholder for the real thing to show up.

His eyes start to droop and he can’t say for how long he’s been walking. Has he even looked for any signs? He might’ve walked past Okhema already, for all he knows. Maybe he should turn back. Mydei is so heavy. Tribbie’s breaths are too hot against his clammy skin and he wants to sleep. His insides feel hollowed out; and like they’ve turned to stone at the same time.

If not for the flame-chase, he thinks, none of you would’ve given me the time of day.

“Heave-ho,” he rasps with a hollow voice, “duck, duck, go.”

His eyes sting with tears, but they don’t fall. It’s better this way. The Deliverer wouldn’t cry, would they? So he can’t, either. Keep going. Just always keep going. Just one more step, always just one more step. That’s all it takes.

I think you would’ve liked him.

Sweat rolls down his neck, and his arms start to really hurt from all the weight. Even Tribbie’s body pressed into his chest provides no comfort any longer and he longs to get rid of her. But he fears, if he puts either of them down, he’ll have no strength left to fasten them to himself anymore.

A person worthy of love and trust, with no flaws or faults, and the only person that could fulfil Era Nova.

“Then that’s who I’ll be,” he whispers, “I’ll be the Deliverer.”

Would Cyrene laugh at him, if she saw him like this? Would anyone even recognise him anymore? He can’t go home anymore. If he dies, all of Aedes Elysiae dies with him. He’s so cold. He wonders if mom baked any bread today. He misses it. He misses sitting on the roof with Cyrene and he misses feeding the fishes some bread. Would she miss him too, if she were in his stead? Aglaea wouldn’t have needed to waste so much time on training her how to speak, either.

It was a little embarrassing. He puts a hand on the wooden beam. He’s wearing a gauntlet. He’s wearing a gauntlet? Didn’t he have a sword? How odd.

He hears sounds behind him. Steps. A lot of steps, actually. There aren’t supposed to be any steps. He closes his fist around the wooden beam. He has a gauntlet. His sword is gone. Is his cargo in danger? When the steps are close enough, he fastens his grip on the wooden beam and he pulls it out of the ground in one fell swoop, whipping it around to hit whoever has approached him. “Lord Phainon! Calm down!”

That voice... it sounds familiar. It could be a trick. It could be like Livia. Nobody will harm the cargo on his back. So he ignores the voice and ducks low, to feint towards his left. He doesn’t get countered this time, but

something akin to threads weave around him, hindering him from moving. He tries not to panic, but the dread is rising in his chest regardless.

He flexes his muscles and he won’t be stopped. They want what he’s carrying? Then they have to kill him first. It’s just odd, that these threads feel familiar somehow, but they feel wrong. “Stop resisting, Phainon!”

If he were able to maim one, however... strangely enough, they seem to be attached to each other. He’s never seen that tactic before. No matter.

“Snowy, we’re here now. It’s okay. You can let go. You did good, Snowy.”

“It’s alright, Lord Phainon. We’ll take you there, I promise. We’ll take you to Okhema.”

He still shouldn’t give in. He should refuse, and be on his way again. But he knows these voices. He trusts these voices. And despite it all, they’re still so gentle with him, as if he deserves it.

Why didn’t you save us?

“Mydei,” he says, “he got... I tried, I did... his head, I tried, and, and Tribbie, she... she’s warm.”

“Don’t worry, Lord Phainon, I’m here. I’ll take care of them. You carried them so far, let me carry them for you now.”

But he shouldn’t allow that, right? These burdens are his to bear, and if he can’t even carry this, then how could he ever hope to bear the world? He’s so tired. Maybe it’s okay to give in just once, right? It’s going to be okay, right? He can still be the Deliverer.

“Alright,” he agrees with a weak voice, and a warm hand grabs his, pulling him forward. He goes willingly. The others are behind him, and he tries to not raise his hackles at that. He knows them. He knows these voices. They won’t hurt him. It’s just hard to... remember that.

He blinks, and he stands in Okhema. Looking up, he can see Kephale in the distance. So, he’s... made it? He’s made it back to Okhema?

“Lord Phainon,” the gentle voice urges him on, “please keep following me.”

He simply nods and follows two bobbing pigtails. He knows them, doesn’t he? Things are way too fuzzy in his head. There’s a bed in front of him, and he blankly stares at it.

“Lord Phainon,” the pigtails speak, “please put Lord Mydei on the bed. Lady Aglaea can take Lady Tribbie, alright?”

He doesn’t react when Tribbie is taken out of the makeshift sling. His chest feels cold, all of sudden, but he’s been given a task. He reaches behind him to hold onto Mydei, while he undoes the knots in the front, until the coat flutters to the ground. He leans to the side and almost topples over, as he needs to adjust to Mydei’s weight with only one arm. He hesitates for a moment, as he goes about how to best do this. He walks over to the bed and turns his torso, trying to slide Mydei onto the bed as gently as he can. Looking at him for the first time again after titans know how long, he was worried that Mydei’s head would’ve... slipped off, or something, but it looks—good? He hopes, at least.

“You must be hurt, Lord Phainon. But, can you tell me what happened? Anything I need to look out for?”

Hurt? No, he’s not hurt. He can’t remember. He shakes his head and then turns to Tribbie, pointing at her.

“She... I think, I think she has a concussion but she. She didn’t stop breathing.” Maybe he should’ve tried harder waking her up. Didn’t he read somewhere that someone with a concussion shouldn’t sleep?

He turns back to Mydei. “He... I think... I think he got concussed too. He didn’t. He didn’t see the monster. I, I tried, but I... I didn’t have anything. I didn’t know. I didn’t—I didn’t want him to come back without a head.”

“Thank you, Lord Phainon,” pigtails—no, no, Hyacine—says, “and what about you? You’ve done so great, Lord Phainon, please let me take care of you now.”

Take care of him? No. No, she has more important things to take care of. He shakes his head again, tired. How long has it been? It would be embarrassing if he’d only wandered for like, two days.

“It’s... it’s fine,” he says, rubbing his temple, “but I... I think I should sleep. I’m—I’m sorry for attacking. We, we were ambushed, I think, before, and I —“ He stops himself by coughing hard and he slams his fist on his chest.

“Don’t worry yourself, child,” thread-weaver—no, no, Aglaea—says from behind him, “rest first, would you? The report can wait a little longer. But please answer Hyacine first. Where are you hurt?”

She’s asking like she’s expecting an injury. How could he be her most trusted warrior if he always returns with injuries? He can’t remember the last time Castorice got hurt. But it would be hard to deny all the blood, wouldn’t it? Not to mention his behaviour... he’s so tired.

“How long were we gone?” He asks instead.

“We lost contact with Tribbie about a week ago. It was hard to locate you, Snowy. You move really fast, you know?”

“Sorry,” he apologises, abashed. “I... got shot in the leg, I think. They’re all numb. B—but Mydei and Lady Tribbie should come first. I’m fine. I can just sleep it off, yeah?”

“No, Lord Phainon. Please let me have a look at it, alright? I know you must be tired, but please—for my own sake of mind.”

She’s not even guilt-tripping him. Well, maybe a little, but she means well. And his leg is fine, isn’t it? As long as she leaves his midriff alone—he closes his eyes and nods, sitting down on a chair. He won’t let himself relax just yet, because then how the hell would he get back up? Hyacine settles in next to him and she gently cuts a hole in his pants to inspect the impact wound. Huh... the shaft must’ve broken off at some point, he didn’t even notice. He should’ve pulled the arrow out before... now poor Hyacine will need to dig it out.

“Are there any other symptoms besides the numbness, Lord Phainon? Weakness, perhaps, or some seizing?”

“No,” he replies, “just numb. I think I rolled my ankle at some point? I can’t remember...”

Hyacine nods, and she gingerly takes his ankles in hand, rolling them both carefully, testing. Maybe he should try to give some rough report to Aglaea, but he just can’t bring himself to do so. He should, he knows, because he has downtime while Hyacine works, but... he’s so tired. Aglaea will understand, right?

“I think it will be alright,” Hyacine then says, standing up. “I will get you some cream for your ankle and the wound, please apply them at least twice a day. It seems it was truly just a numbing poison, even though I wonder how it persisted for so long... ideally, it should go away on its own in a couple days. If the numbness persists or gets worse please come back to see me right away, Lord Phainon.”

He just nods. Did she get the arrowhead out? He can’t remember. Doesn’t matter anyway, right? It’ll be fine. He can look later. He feels Hyacine’s

hand on his forehead and he tries hard not to flinch. He’s not usually this jumpy, is he?

“Hmm,” she concludes, “you do have a bit of a fever. Cassie, can you make sure he gets home safe? I want to look at Lady Tribbie and Lord Mydei now.”

“Of course,” Castorice says, “can you stand, Lord Phainon?”

He groans, and pushes himself up. He slips the cream into his pocket and turns towards the door. He feels too light, like he might float away. A week... it can’t have been that long. Maybe time was distorted in the temple? But Tribbie didn’t mention losing her connection to Trianne and Trinnon... weird. But in the end, what does it matter?

“Lord Phainon,” Castorice says, “you are a terrific fighter.”

“Huh?”

“I mean,” she laughs, “facing off against you truly made me fear for my life. I keep thinking that if you’d had your sword, we wouldn’t have stood a chance. Not even Lady Aglaea’s threads could stop you.”

Oh... right. “I’m—sorry. Did I hurt you? It wasn’t my intention, I just—“

“No, no, don’t worry. It just occurred to me that it’s been a long time since I saw you fight. You truly are impressive, Lord Phainon!”

He knows Castorice wouldn’t lie to him. But it still feels like hollow praise. How could he be impressive if he failed to protect both Tribbie and Mydei from harm?

“Miss Castorice,” he says and she turns, smiling. “I would wish to bathe first. I promise I’ll head home straight after, so there’s no need to wait on me.”

“Oh... are you certain? I can wait for you, Lord Phainon! I would offer to assist you, but, well... but I can make sure nobody would disturb you!”

He thinks a little, then nods. “I would appreciate that, Miss Castorice, thank you. I’ll make haste, too. I’m sure there are important things you must be doing, as well.”

“Nothing is more important than you right now, Lord Phainon,” she smiles gently and it almost hurts. But still, he smiles in return and they make their way to the baths. He feels strangely naked without his coat. He can see people try to greet him from afar, but he’s trying hard to ignore them. If he makes eye-contact, he’ll stop and talk to them. A week... it feels so much longer. He feels so much older than when he started. Maybe that feeling will go away once he’s slept. Should he eat something? He’s not very hungry, and maybe Mydei has some stuff still left in his fridge. If he doesn’t... well, he’ll live.

“Lord Phainon,” Castorice turns to him, “will you give me your clothes? I’ll see if I can salvage them... and in the meantime, I’ll bring you something fresh to wear.”

“Oh... no, no, you mustn’t make such an effort for me, Miss Castorice. It’s fine, truly.”

She shakes her head. “I insist. You’ll feel much better wearing fresh clothes, believe me.”

She’s probably right, too. But still... looking at her, though, makes him give up. “Fine,” he relents, “but I think it’s better if you just throw them away. There’s bound to be a lot of blood on there... and, uh. Could you. I, I mean —“

“Yes, I’ll get some of Lord Mydei’s clothes for you, don’t worry,” she laughs. “I’ll be back as soon as I can. Just please don’t fall asleep in the waters, alright?”

He nods and hands her his tattered clothes after he’s undressed. He waits until her steps have faded into silence, and then he dashes into the Hero’s Bath. The wound on his stomach looks—well, he wouldn’t want Hyacine to see it, that’s for certain. It started to half-heal, but the edges are all red and puffy and he still retains the heaviness from it. He taps one foot into the

water first; an old-born habit, before he sinks into the bath. This bath always made sure that the Chrysos Heirs would never fall to the corruption of the black tide. Truth be told, he’s not sure how it works or why this water specifically can do it, but why ask questions nobody could answer anyway?

However, as he sinks into the waters, his blood begins to burn. He chokes on nothing, gasping for air he can’t take in and it feels like his body is trying to devour itself. He can’t—he can’t be corrupted, right? No, no, that can’t be... it’s got to be something else. But the pain keeps pulsing, keeps rushing through his very core and oh, he burns. Still, he tries to endure, because surely, if he stays in just long enough, the waters will burn the corruption away, won’t they?

However, after too short a time, he throws himself out of the bath, convulsing on the floor. Oh, how pathetic, but it hurts so much. He curls up on himself, wrapping his arms around his stomach, barely caring where his towel goes. After the initial pain has passed, he uncurls and looks at his hands. There’s blood on them, but the blood is—it’s black. He’s not supposed to bleed black. Wasn’t the water meant to cleanse him? Why did it burn him instead? He whimpers and curls back up, waiting for the pain to pass. He has to get up before Castorice returns. He has to... oh, he’s so tired.

“...non! Lord Phainon!”

He blinks his eyes open to gaze upon the blurry vision of the baths. Huh? What happened? He turns his head towards the voice and blinks lazily. When did Castorice come back?

“Miss... Castorice...?”

“Lord Phainon! Are you alright? Should I go get Hyacine? Was the water too hot? I, I came back and you were lying on the floor!”

He blinks and turns his head away again. It hurts. He’s still tired. “No, no...” he reassures her, “I’m just—I’m just tired. Maybe a bath was a bad idea, I’m sorry. Do you... have some clothes for me?”

Castorice nods, lifting a red robe in her hands. Oh, she really did get some of Mydei’s clothes... how nice. He nods in response and sits up. Castorice puts the clothes on a nearby chair, so not to get them wet and then turns around to give him some privacy. He heaves himself over to the chair, trying to stifle a groan. It takes entirely too long to put the garments on, but ah, well. He’s allowed, right?

“I’m. I’m done, Miss Castorice. Forgive me for keeping you waiting.”

“No, no!” She’s quick to say. “I’m sorry I can’t help more. But, if you’d allow me...”

With a bright smile, she extends her wooden hand. Right, he remembers making that in the Grove. It’s nice to see she still has them. He laughs a little, and takes her hand, allowing her to lead him. He still can’t close his eyes, in case she has to stop suddenly, but at least he won’t need to concentrate on walking like this.

“This is Mydei’s house,” he says when they arrive.

“Yes,” she agrees, “it’s where you wanted to go, isn’t it?”

“Fair enough,” he chuckles. “Thank you, Miss Castorice. Please let Miss Hyacine and Lady Aglaea know I made it here safely? I’ll report to Lady Aglaea tomorrow in full, I promise. If Kephale wills it, Lady Tribbie will have recovered by then, as well.”

She smiles and bows a little. “Of course, Lord Phainon. Please don’t hesitate to contact me or someone else should you require anything. I’ll come by tomorrow again to check on you, if we haven’t heard from you by then. Rest well, Lord Phainon.”

He nods in response and walks inside the house. The air is a little stale, but he’s lacking the strength to open the windows. Tomorrow he’ll do it, he swears. But right now, all he wants to do is sleep, so he sprawls over Mydei’s bed and tries to fall asleep.

However, as tired as he is, his mind still races. He’s still not sure what exactly happened in that damned temple, or what the purpose of it even was. These mirrors... how do they work? Why did they work? And what did they want? He doesn’t understand; and these symbols—these symbols he’s never seen before, but that still feel so familiar. Where did the monster come from all of a sudden? Was it all just some elaborate ploy? But this seems way above their usual abilities... his head hurts. He’s still wearing Mydei’s gauntlet. He hopes that Mydei wakes up soon; that he didn’t mess up or that Hyacine can fix it. He really tried, didn’t he...?

He’ll deal with—with the corruption tomorrow. If he just takes enough baths, then it’ll go away. He can’t tell Aglaea or Hyacine; he doesn’t want to worry them even further. Tomorrow, he will stand tall before the Lady Goldweaver and report to her what happened and he’ll show her the pictures he took and then maybe someone will have some answers and maybe they can blow the place to bits. He’ll apologise to Tribbie and Mydei as soon as they wake up and hopefully, they’ll forgive him. He’ll be upset at Mydei for dying in front of him again and Mydei will scoff and tell him that it’s his fault for not being faster. And then they can forget that forsaken temple and go back to how things were before.

He closes his eyes and falls into uneasy slumber.

“Little Deliverer... you can never reach your destination, for it is nothing but a lie. It’s an everlasting labyrinth of mirrors that reflect you a thousand-fold. For freedom; for truth; for deliverance, one must shatter the mirror. But are you strong enough? Do you yet burn hot enough? The ever-raging flame inside the cavity of your chest... when will it sweep the land like wildfire? The Scourge of Amphoreus will ascend into the heavens, for to slay a god, one must become a god themselves. Crown yourself in their golden blood and destroy every blight in the universe. O Khaslana, son of Amphoreus, do you still remember them? Sing, o aeons, for your eternal hymn will shatter under the footsteps of his golden rage.

Little Deliverer, do you still remember why you started your journey?”

Mydeimos can hear the wind before anything else. He’s not sure where he is or what’s even happened, but—the wind sounds soft and he can smell no blood, so it can’t be a battlefield. He tries to remember but all he comes up with are blanks. Hadn’t he been with Phainon? Where’s Phainon? He can’t feel anyone holding his hand or hitting his chest. Where is the Deliverer?

“...dei?”

A voice. He’s not sure who it belongs to, but voices are good. He tries to open his eyes, and he groans. This never used to be so damn hard. If Phainon were here, it’d be easier. Maybe it’ll help if he deludes the Deliverer by his side.

“Hey now, Mydeimos! Can’t even open your eyes properly? Guess that means I’ll win our blinking competition! Bow to your champion!”

Asshole. Under extreme difficulties, Mydei manages to open his eyes and is greeted by the blurry visage of the sky. Blurry blobs shove themselves into his field of sight immediately and he grumbles, frowning. Can a man not wake in peace?

“Little Dei!”

He blinks a couple times before turning his head, staring straight into Tribbie’s face.

“You,” he rasps, “...Deliverer?”

“He’ll be by soon,” a new voice says and he blinks, identifying the new blob as Hyacine. She smiles warmly at him, coming closer. “How do you feel?”

“Groggy,” he replies: his body feels like it’s made out of lead. “How long was I out? What even happened?”

“Hmm, about three weeks I think? That’s when we brought you back here, anyway. I have to admit, you had me worried! It’s never taken you so long to come back!”

Three weeks? She’s right, it should never take this long... the longest it’s taken so far had been a day. How in the world could it have been three weeks? Oh, Phainon must be so mad.

“Snowy said that you... you got beheaded, Dei.”

He stills and turns his head to look at Trinnon. Oh, all three of them are here. “What... did you say?”

“Please, Dei, don’t make me repeat myself. It’s what Snowy told us.”

“Yes,” Hyacine nods, “she’s right. And it—it really happened. Lord Phainon did his best to... re-attach you to your body and given his limited knowledge and limited tools, he performed spectacularly. However, it was still gruesome to see. I keep hoping that the shock made Lord Phainon forget the details.”

Mydei gingerly touches his neck and he is met with—a band of sorts? He frowns and feels around it. If he’s not mistaken...

“Lord Phainon used his leather band as a stabiliser. I wanted to give it back to him but he started panicking when I went to undo the clasp so I opted to leave it on. It’s still odd to see him without it.”

“What happened?”

“According to Snowy, something knocked all of you out and gave you and Tribbie a concussion,” Trianne supplies, “then he heard some monsters and went to fight them. You apparently woke up and went to check on Snowy but you... didn’t see the monster and died. Snowy took care of the rest of the monsters, punched you a way out and wandered around until we could find him. Snowy was scary, you know? Trianne really thought he’d kill Agy and Little Cas! Everyone’s real glad he’s our friend.”

Phainon... all alone against an entire horde of enemies, while also having watched Mydei fall? However much time has passed, Phainon will not be in a good state. How is Mydei going to make up for this?

“Did he get wounded? Is he alright?”

“Honestly,” Hyacine sighs, looking uncomfortable, “I was hoping you could help me with that. He hates to bother me, when he never could bother me. I keep telling myself that it’s just stress and the like, but—I’m only two steps away from chaining him here to force-feed him. Seeing you up and about will do wonders! Now, do you want to try standing up? I and Lord Phainon did some exercises with you while you were sleeping, so let’s see if they’ve helped.”

He nods, taking her hands as she helps him up. Yes, his legs definitely feel like he hasn’t used them in a while. He can stand, but... it feels rather wobbly. However, it shouldn’t take long to regain functionality in them. Hyacine asks him to move his arms, his torso and most importantly, his neck. It all feels fine; if a little stiff. He should definitely ease himself back into training slowly. Knowing Phainon, he’ll have overdone it while Mydei had been gone, so going slow would probably do him some good, too.

“...Mydei?”

His eyes widen and he turns his head at that voice. There, at the entrance of the courtyard, stands Phainon and by Nikador, he looks terrible. Eyes sunken in, cheeks hollowed out, skin pale. He wears most of his usual get-up, but instead of his white coat, he has one of Mydei’s robes wrapped around him; and his right arm dons Mydei’s gauntlet.

He’s so beautifully perfect it’s unfair.

“Deliverer,” he whispers and he lets go of Hyacine, to walk over to Phainon before he simply breaks out in a run. Phainon himself can’t avert his eyes and he takes small steps towards Mydei, clearly not believing what he sees. Mydei slams into Phainon with all his might, absolutely uncaring of where they are and the impact shock sends Phainon backwards on his back as Mydei ravages his mouth.

Desperate, his hands hold onto every part of Phainon they can reach and after slight hesitation due to shock, Phainon wraps his arms around Mydei, returning his kiss in kind.

“Deliverer,” Mydei pants into Phainon’s open mouth, “oh, my Deliverer.”

“Mydei,” Phainon breathes, “it’s really...? Are you—are you okay? Your, your neck, is it fine? I... Mydei, I—“

“Shush,” Mydei whispers, kissing him again. “I am well. Titans, Deliverer, you should wear nothing but my clothes ever again.”

Phainon blinks, frowns in confusion and then laughs.

“Oh Mydei,” he sobs, “oh Mydei.”

“Is it really okay?” Phainon asks for the nth time. “Maybe you should go back and—“

“Deliverer,” Mydei interrupts him. “You were there when Hyacine said I’m good to go. I’m even still wearing your little collar, so what’s there to worry about?”

“It’s not a collar...”

Mydei laughs softly and turns over from where they lie in bed and he gently cups Phainon’s cheek. Tomorrow, he’ll make a meal plan for both of them.

He’s sure Aglaea will agree not to send them out on mission for at least two weeks.

“You still wear my gauntlet.”

“Huh? Oh, yeah... sorry, it, uh, it became kind of a habit. I, uh, I put it on to... do stuff. And then, ah, then I punched a wall with it. Sorry, I’ll take it off right away—“

“Deliverer,” he reprimands, “it’s fine. I keep your collar, you keep my gauntlet. It looks good on you. You, however, look terrible. Has it truly been three weeks?”

“Yes,” Phainon admits after a short pause. “Longer than that, I think. I’m not sure how much time passed after I left the temple.”

“Speaking of it—did Aglaea send someone there to investigate?”

Phainon remains quiet for a bit, idly playing with the gauntlet in a way that tells Mydei it’s become a habit. “No,” the man then says, “I told her about it but when she sent people there... Mydei, there was nothing. Nothing. Even the pictures I took are gone. It’s like the place never existed. I wanted to go back myself, to confirm, but Lady Aglaea strictly forbade me from leaving Okhema.”

Phainon looks genuinely distressed and Mydei frowns. It’s impossible for a place to just straight up vanish, isn’t it? Especially if it’s underground. Mydei reaches out his hand and brushes it through Phainon’s hair. It’s not as soft as he remembers and just another sign how easy it is for Phainon to neglect himself.

“We’ll go together,” he says, “when we’re both better.”

“Okay... wait! I’m fine. I didn’t get hurt; I just ran a little fever for a while.”

Mydei doesn’t mention Hyacine’s concern to him. He sighs and moves his hand to Phainon’s left arm, wrapped in a thick bandage.

“Does it not ache?”

“I... it’s nothing, Mydeimos, I promise. I even put some cream on it, so it’s fine, isn’t it?”

Oh, cream. Wonderful. The famous miracle cream, said to cure any and all ailments. But well, at least it’s something. Gently, he lifts the arm and reaches over, pressing a kiss on the bandage. It’s not spotted, at least, so he’ll take that little mercy.

“I’m sorry,” he says, “that I wasn’t there to take care of you.”

“It’s fine,” Phainon mutters, but he doesn’t tug his arm away. Mydei sighs and closes his eyes. Phainon smells the same and honestly, he shouldn’t miss it so, having slept all this time. He still can’t wrap his head around the fact it’s been three whole weeks.

“Are you... really okay? I know what Hyacine said, but—“

“Come,” Mydei replies, “feel for yourself, then.”

Hesitant, Phainon turns over and gently presses his palm against Mydei’s neck. He rubs his thumb into the skin and strokes along the side reverently. Mydei simply watches Phainon as he does so. He looks tired—when has he slept last? He wishes Phainon would put himself first sometimes, because what good would it do if he were to collapse in the streets? It’s alright, though, because Mydei is going to make sure the Deliverer gets enough rest, now.

“I have to tell you something,” Phainon whispers, cradling his hand back to himself. Mydei already misses the contact. He nods at Phainon, urging him to keep going.

“I—a while ago, Zacharias kissed me.”

Maybe Mydei should be furious. Maybe he should get angry, but instead he feels—calm, almost.

“Did you like it?”

“No,” Phainon replies, “I don’t know. I was sick and drunk, so it’s a little blurry. I just—if you want to go—“

Mydei reaches over for his face and pulls him close, kissing him sweet and gentle on the mouth. It’s a closed-mouth kiss, born from devotion and reverence, not their usual fire and desire. Phainon doesn’t put his hands on Mydei’s body, and he is hesitant in returning the kiss proper.

“This,” Mydei whispers against his lips, “is how I and Hephaestion kissed. Do you remember what our first kiss was like?”

Phainon’s eyes are always so big, even when they’re clouded from too little sleep and too much stress. Looking into these eyes, and Mydei doesn’t even need Kephale’s Eternal Dawn Device. He’s got his own little pocket sun right here.

“Like, our first kiss or our first kiss?”

Mydei pouts. He and Phainon have had a physical relationship long before they’ve had a romantic one, so they fucked first and kissed later. Of course, during sex they had kissed sometimes, but it hadn’t meant anything back then. The Deliverer is such an ass to bring that back.

“Don’t ruin the mood, Deliverer. So: do you still remember our first kiss?”

Phainon nods, and smiles deviously. Mydei smirks and pulls Phainon back in, pressing his lips against the other man’s again. He starts slow, cradling Phainon’s face in his hands and the man finally, finally puts his hands on Mydei’s chest, where they belong. The tension ebbs out of Mydei’s shoulders and he pulls Phainon closer; flush to his chest before he moves his hand to grab a fistful of snow-white hair. “Then don’t fret, little Deliverer,” Mydei soothes, “because only I can give you this.”

Phainon huffs out a breathy laugh. “You forgive me, then?”

Mydei gently caresses his cheek. Phainon, for some suicidal reason, likes to jump from roof to roof. Like a hero in the stories, the man would claim. He’s given all of Okhema a heart attack at least once and Mydei is sure Aglaea doesn’t even see it anymore. Anyway, he’s dared Mydei countless times to see who can jump further and even though Mydei does not share Phainon’s tendencies, he still agreed. In this world and the next, you are my only equal; the one person I will always yearn for—to fight, to love, to hold, it doesn’t matter. You could burn the world and I would know you have purpose. Maybe I would not agree, but I trust none more than you. I am yours, no matter what and I will walk to the ends of this earth if I have to. *

Mydei wakes slowly. His pillow is breathing. In all honesty, that’s rather unusual. His pillows are usually stuffed with feathers, not lungs. He blinks a couple times before he lifts his head to be greeted by Phainon’s sleeping

face. Oh. That is most unusual. Eternal insomniac Phainon sleeping in for once?

Smiling, Mydei leans on his arms and watches Phainon sleep. He looks better asleep, although the dark circles under his eyes stand out. Gently, Mydei brushes his thumb over Phainon’s cheek and thinks about a suitable meal plan. His general plan is to make sure Phainon eats, and then to get him napping. The more he rests, the better his body will be able to recover. He bends down and nuzzles his nose against the Deliverer. Phainon pulls a face in his sleep and turns his head away.

Chuckling softly, Mydei sits up. He’s tempted to remove the large bandage around the man’s torso, but he refrains. He’s seen it last night, but because he hadn’t wanted to ruin the mood—and because he believed it to be from Phainon’s self-harm—he had left it unmentioned. Now, though... it is a rather large bandage and Phainon has never resorted to his stomach before. What made him do it? The cuts on his arms and legs are by no means old, but they aren’t as numerous that he would have run out of space. Maybe it was desperation? After all, he doesn’t know what really happened—and some part of him believes nobody knows.

“Whatever am I going to do with you,” Mydei whispers and brushes his hand through Phainon’s hair. It’s a little oily and Mydei is hardly surprised that Phainon straight up forgot to take care of himself. No matter. Mydei is back now, and the Deliverer will be cared for, whether he likes it or not.

He leans down again and presses a soft kiss against Phainon’s slightly heated forehead. It’s alright, Phainon runs hot a lot of times. Again, nothing a good rest won’t fix. Hesitating, Mydei gets out of bed and quietly dresses himself. He washes down quickly and then heads into the kitchen to prepare some breakfast. He’d make honey cakes, but since he’s not sure when the Deliverer will wake, he decides against it. He makes sandwiches instead, and in the worst scenario, the Deliverer will have to suffer through some sogginess. He’ll live, regardless.

He places the plate on the counter, nicely visible, and he heads back into the bedchamber for a spell; just to see if Phainon had woken. The man has

scarcely moved, and Mydei huffs with a smile. Just how ragged has he run himself?

“I’ll return soon,” he promises, “eat the sandwich I made, or I’ll choke it down your throat.”

Successfully threatened, he turns and leaves. His first order of business is the detachment. Possibly four weeks out of commission must’ve run them down, and he must make appearances to placate them. He speaks with a few people, and each one sighs in relief upon seeing him, but they all promise they have done him proud in his absence. He wonders how much Aglaea has let seep through—do they know he perished? Do they believe him having been on a mission? He won’t ask, as not to risk expose himself, and perhaps Aglaea can shine light on it later. He finds Krateros as a last stop.

“My lord,” he is greeted and Mydei nods in acknowledgment.

“Krateros. How have things been? The people tell me nothing but good news.”

“Yes, nothing much happened in your absence. That Deliverer of yours helped us out whenever he could, although I must admit—he would not speak of your whereabouts, and he himself looked worn thin. Indulge your old teacher?”

Hm. So his death had been kept secret. Perhaps it was for the best. “Not currently,” he answers honestly, “I wish to speak to the Goldweaver first. Since—returning, I haven’t had the chance. But rest assured, once I am able, you will get the truth.”

Krateros sighs deep, and Mydei didn’t expect anything else. It must be frustrating, to be kept in the dark like this. But he finds himself agreeing with Aglaea—he, too, is hesitant to share past events. How would they react, if Mydeimos the Undying has stayed dead for weeks when normally he stays dead for minutes? It might be too frightening—they rely on his immortality more than he does.

“Very well then, my lord. And that Deliverer boy of yours... is he faring well?”

Mydei crosses his arms. “He wears himself thin as usual, especially considering I was not here to knock some sense into him. Fret not, teacher. I am surprised you ask after his well-being—do you not consider him the same as the rest of the Okheman scum?”

Krateros clenches his jaw. “He gained your respect, my lord, so he gained mine as well. In this city; I’d be a fool to turn a helping hand away, no matter how much it grates me.”

“He is an Outlander, much like us, and you know this,” Mydei counters, “if not for him, the Goldweaver would have us placed in the pig stalls.”

“Little lion!”

“Agy, I... I got him. I should—“

No.

He looks toward the doorway Aglaea and Ciper are half-standing in. From here, he can only see half of Castorice. His feet move of their own accord and he doesn’t look; he doesn’t turn his head. He can’t see Hyacine, can’t see the bed, but he can hear her hefty sobs.

No.

No.

If Phainon didn’t eat the sandwich, Mydei is going to push it down his throat regardless. The sandwich is half-finished. He doesn’t want to turn his head. If he doesn’t look, it’s not real. “What,” he asks flatly, “happened?”

“The,” Hyacine starts to hiccup, “the corruption hic ran so deep, Dei hic there was hic nothing I could do!”

Cipher slinks back a little, ashamed, and Aglaea holds her tight, not saying anything.

Dead.

No.

Phainon can’t be dead, Phainon can never be dead. There has to be... there has to be something he can do. He is Mydeimos the Undying, the Conqueror, eternal victor of the battlefield. And yet here he stands, rooted to the spot, and he’s never been weaker.

“Out of the way!” A new voice shouts, but Mydei hardly registers it. Phainon, dead and silent on the bed.

“Let me through, woman!”

A blurry flash of green rushes past his peripheral vision and Mydei blinks. This is... Anaxagoras. The great scholar of the grove, and Phainon’s beloved teacher.

“Phainon of Aedes Elysiae!”

He leans close to Phainon’s still form, noses almost touching but Phainon does not move. Anaxagoras balls his hands into fist and tension flows out of his shoulders; and he almost sags.

“Pro—hic—Professor Anaxa...”

He pays her no mind.

“No matter,” he says, mainly to himself, “I can fix this. It’ll be an easy feat. Defying death itself? Ha! Nothing is impossible with alchemy.”

He gets up and hurries out of the room, only to be stopped by Aglaea’s hand on his arm. She’s not holding him tight, but he still stops regardless.

“Anaxagoras,” she says, voice as old as her years, “you are aware I cannot let you continue.”

“Is he not your golden boy, Aglaea? Are you content with his still body? I, for one—“

“What, Anaxagoras. Use alchemy to return him to life? You sacrificed your eye to simply glimpse at your sister again. What would the cost be for a life? Your brain? Your body? Your soul? Your heart? Phainon,” she stops herself, taking a deep breath and pulling Cipher closer, “did not simply perish. He fell to corruption. I wish—I would throw you in golden fire if it would bring him back, Anaxagoras, and I am aware you’d do the same to me. I would let you. Anaxagoras slightly turns his head towards her, not answering. He lowers his head and turns his body towards the room again.

“If he would live,” he quietly says before stepping back into the room. He passes straight by Mydei and halts before Castorice, holding out his hand.

Castorice closes her eyes and nods in thanks. Anaxagoras lingers a little, before he walks around the bed and kneels down next to Hyacine.

“Hyacine,” he tells her, “I know you did all you could.”

She lifts her head from the bed, tears still streaking down her face and she hiccups, throwing herself in his arms. She wails against his chest, not being able to form coherent words or phrases, and Anaxagoras simply rubs her back, pressing his face against her hair.

Mydei turns his gaze back on Phainon. Corruption… now he understands the purpose of the bandage. He should’ve looked. He should’ve looked, and maybe—maybe what? Suck it out of him?

“I don’t understand,” he says, “how did it take this long?”

“You’re right,” Hyacine agrees, still sniffling, but having shed most of her tears for now. “While we Heirs are somewhat resistant to the black tide, we’re hardly immune. “Maybe,” Hyacine sniffles, “but with how aggressive the corruption usually is, that sounds like a non-possibility.”

“He didn’t transform, either,” Cipher remarks from Aglaea’s side. They have interwoven their fingers.

“That’s right, so… in short, I don’t know. It… it doesn’t even matter. If he’d only come to me, maybe I could’ve…”

“Can you clean the corruption now?” Mydei asks.

Hyacine blinks, then looks down at Phainon. “I… think so? Are you worried he might turn?”

Mydei shakes his head. If Phainon didn’t turn until now, he never will. But he… he can’t let this be the way it ends. He’s immortal. He should use it.

“The River of Souls is stagnant,” he says instead.

“Ah,” Anaxagoras nods, “his soul might not have yet reached the afterlife. What a peculiar thought, Mydeimos. I see why Phainon is so enraptured with you. Let’s make haste, then.”

He stands up and looks at Phainon, reaching forth a hand to brush through Phainon’s hair. Mydei regrets not having taking a bath together yesterday.

“However,” Anaxagoras warns, “a soul is a delicate thing and unlike you, us plebeians cannot force our soul to turn back. How will you transport him back?”

Mydei falls silent. He hadn’t thought that far.

Anaxagoras eyes him silently, and then he reaches inside his coat, procuring an empty vial.

“This,” he states in great grandeur, “is a soul phial that I just happen to have on me. Once you locate Phainon’s soul, all you need to do is convince him to go into the phial and then you return to life as usual. Surely that’s something you can manage?”

“I never heard of a soul phial before.”

“It’s a real thing,” Cipher says quickly, “I see them in rich guys’ vaults like all the time. They don’t sell, so I never take them, but that’s what they are. Stores one good soul just right, just like grove boy here said.”

Mydei frowns. He’s not convinced. But why would they lie to him? He reaches out and takes the little bottle. It looks so unassuming and— Phainon’s soul is meant to fit inside that? He supposes souls aren’t corporal, so it shouldn’t be a problem, but still…

“Don’t think so much, Mydeimos,” Anaxagoras continues, “or is that simple task too much for you? I would go in your stead, but why ease

Aglaea’s life of this burden?”

“No, it’s fine,” Mydei says and closes his fingers around the vial. He can do this. He won’t give up. He’s lost all his friends, he will not lose Phainon as well. Phainon is too important.

“Castorice,” he turns to her, “will you grant me death’s embrace?”

Hesitating, she clasps her hands tighter together. He knows it’s cruel to ask it of her. Phainon is still wearing one of Mydei’s gauntlets. He takes a step closer to her.

“I will return,” he re-assures her and she turns her head away.

“I know,” her voice is tightly pressed, “but it isn’t easy. What if my touch… is final, Lord Mydei?”

“Then I will gladly take my last breath in the embrace of a friend.”

Her eyes widen and she looks up at him. Steeling herself with a steadying breath, she nods and steps forward, embracing him. He closes his arms around her, hugging her close.

“Your hands are warm,” he says, feeling death lap at his heels, “one day, the Deliverer will not be able to stop holding them.”

The last thing he feels is her squeezing him tight. Her body against his is such a comforting thing. He thinks he understands now, when she speaks of the flowers at the end of the westwind. Maybe one of the first things he’ll do in Era Nova is hugging Castorice.

Mydei wakes slowly. He doesn’t remember falling asleep, if he’s honest. He groans and sits up, rubbing his head. What… was he doing? There’s

something nagging at the back of his head. Maybe it’s just a headache. No, that’s not right.

“Mydeimos!”

He blinks and looks over, seeing Hephaestion waving at him from the camp they set up. Right… he remembers that. He doesn’t really, but… it doesn’t feel strange to him, either. He frowns, rubs his temple and gets up to walk over to them.

“Are you alright? That nap knocked you out, huh?”

“No naptime could defeat me.”

“Of course not!” Peucesta is quick to proclaim. “The mighty lion conquers naptime in one fell swoop!”

Mydeimos frowns. That sounds an awful lot like mockery. However, he decides to let it fly. These are his friends, and it was a jest, anyhow. Mydeimos settles in next to Hephaestion and observes the—camp. It feels odd, somehow. There’s fish on the fire. His friends never used to favour fish... he has to admit he is partial to it, after having sustained on nothing but sea creatures for the first years of his life. So why...?

Let’s get married—

“We should make haste,” he says, “to Okhema.”

“Okhema?” Leonnius asks. “Have you set your eye on the holy city, Mydeimos? I’ve no doubt we can do it, but taking it will be difficult.”

Taking it? Frowning, he lifts his head. He’s never said anything about seizing it, has he?

“No... they are our allies. On the flame-chase journey.”

“My, Mydeimos,” Perdikkas worries, “have you caught a fever? The Holy City has been our enemy since ancient times.”

“I know,” Mydei insists, “I’ve not taken ill. Okhema is our ally; has been for a long time.”

“Perhaps he’s had a dream,” Ptolemy muses, “of distant days in distant realities?”

“No, no, I believe Mydeimos,” Hephaestion says, smiling, “if he declares Okhema our ally, then so they will be—whether they want to or not. Right?”

Mydeimos is slow to nod. Right. Only—that’s not how. An alliance cannot be forced, for if it is forced, it is no other than servitude. Everything feels... wrong, somehow, as if there was a thick fog cloud over his mind. Hadn’t he had a mission? Something important?

He’s missing his right gauntlet for some reason. He doesn’t remember unclasping it and putting it away. Someone... took it, didn’t they? But he feels no panic rising at the thought; more like quiet content. Like he’s pleased by it. Like his missing gauntlet is staking a claim somewhere.

He flexes his fingers. Something’s wrong.

—once tomorrow comes.

“Where’s Phainon?”

“Impressive,” an unknown face says behind him. Mydei had not even heard them approach, so his hackles rise and he jumps about and around, raising his arms. Before him stands a black-clad swordsman, but Mydei can’t make the face out. The voice is—odd, almost familiar, but he still can’t place it.

“I truly thought I would have to shatter the memory to free you from it.”

“Who are you?”

The swordsman remains silent, face turned towards him. Oddly enough, he seems to think about the question. Seeing as he does not raise his sword, Mydei lowers his fists as well. It’d be best if he would not try to engage

with an enemy he can’t read properly—especially on an important mission like his own.

“Khaos,” the swordsman settles on, “it will serve well enough.”

“Khaos,” Mydei repeats and it feels odd on his tongue. Everything is odd. It never used to be like this. Castorice’s embrace cannot have played such a huge factor, can it? No matter, he’s better off not telling her.

“What do you want?”

Khaos remains still, like a statue. “Your mission,” he states, “is of utmost importance. You should see it through.”

His mission... Mydei balls his fists again. How does this Khaos know of Mydei’s mission? And why should it be of utmost importance to him? If Phainon were to remain dead, a new world-bearer would emerge sooner or later, no matter how much the thought hurts.

“How do you know? Why do you care?”

“While you waste breath,” Khaos says, undeterred, “Phainon slips away.” The man turns his head upstream and remains still. It’s eerie, the way he doesn’t even seem to breathe.

“Then get out of my way.”

“I am not an obstacle. Not yet, anyway. Isn’t Strife about forcing a path despite the hindrances?”

“What would you know of Strife? I have no intention to fight you.”

Khaos lowers his head slightly, in a manner that feels achingly familiar and yet, so alien.

“I know more than enough. Tell me instead, where will you go from here?”

Mydei frowns. He’s not sure, actually. In past visits, he would occasionally encounter people from his past, but the chance that those were simply

memories is high. Phainon, however... Phainon’s soul should still be here; and not a memory. He’s just always wandered straight to the end, so to find someone... if Castorice was here, maybe she’d have an idea.

“It is of no concern to you.”

Khaos moves his head up, casting a glance at the sky.

“The golden fields,” Khaos says, “the golden fields of Aedes Elysiae always burn.”

“If you care about Phainon so much, then why not go save him yourself?”

“You can take me there.”

Khaos’ voice sounds almost mocking, when before his cadence had stayed rather monotone. If Mydei had more time, maybe, then he could dedicate the time to properly think about his thoughts; but as things stand, he cannot afford it.

Khaos leans over, still and un-breathing. It’s perhaps the weirdest presence Mydei has felt in a long time and he almost startles when the man lifts his hand—it almost looks like he’s wearing a golden gauntlet, but that must be

He’s not—who was that? There are things he’d rather not think about. He closes his eyes and releases a breath before he looks at the chime. The sound... the rabbits. What the hell? If only he had caught the direction that thing had dashed off to...
