As he dashes across the stagnant land of Styxia, he can hear his mother’s voice call out to him. This isn’t new. In death, she’s the only constant, and he’s never given in to her. “Oh, Mydei,” the voice says and Mydei breathes, but the illusion doesn’t shatter. The tranquillity remains, and it sends shivers down his spine.

If he could have washed up here instead of into the arms of the detachment, maybe he could’ve tried to have a nicer childhood. “She,” Phainon stop-starts for a while, clearly struggling. “She says the book holds my future.”

Mydei frowns. He’s never heard of such a book, but they are currently dead, so he supposes anything goes. And Phainon’s village did worship Oronyx, so the future isn’t too far-fetched a concept.

“What does it say, then? If you’re too scared, I can look for you.”

Phainon moves, putting his hand on the cover. From behind him, the cover is blank and bland. Did it look like that before? No... he’s sure it reminded him of something before. Now it just looks like a sad, forgotten little thing.

“No, no,” Phainon says quickly, “I mean, I was a little worried. What if it said I’ll die to like, I don’t know, the flu? Something embarrassing like that, but I did look, eventually. Guess curiosity killed the Deliverer, huh? Anyway...”

He turns around, and Mydei’s eyes are drawn to the book. How odd. He wanted to look at Phainon first. He frowns, then, when Phainon begins to shuffle through the pages. That... that makes no sense. Why...?

“As you can see,” Phainon sighs, “all the pages are empty. At first I thought it was just a prank, you know, but... Cyrene isn’t even here to see my reaction, and she wouldn’t do that to me. So, what does that mean, then? Why is there nothing there?”

He puts his fingers on a blank page and almost caresses it. His fingernails look nice. They’re well-kept and healthy.

“I’m sure Professor Anaxa would say that this is a sign for endless possibilities—so many that these pages could never hold them, therefore leaving them blank. That’s a nice thought, isn’t it? Even though he pretends not to care, he actually cares so much. Did you know that he found me once, when I tried to kill myself? He didn’t even tell Lady Hyacine or Miss Castorice. He called me stupid, wasteful and lazy, but he stayed by my side until the bleeding stopped. He even made excuses for me the next day; that I had helped him all night with an experiment, which is why I didn’t show up for classes. I slept in his office for a while, and after that, he would occasionally sleep over in my dorm room.”

Solemnly, Phainon turns a page.

“Or,” he says, “it might mean that there simply is no future at all. That I’ll never go beyond this point, that this is where I end. It wouldn’t be so bad, you know, to end here. Everyone else did, too. Did you know, that after—I collected them all and dragged them away; dug graves for all of them? I carved their names onto sticks and placed them nice and neatly. At some points, I wanted to dig a grave for me too, because dying here with them would’ve been kinder. They can’t despise me for not saving them if I, too, died here.”

He turns another page. The wind has stopped and the sound is too loud in that eerie silence surrounding them.

“Or perhaps,” he says, “it’s a future so insignificant that it’s not even worth remembering. That whatever I do, it’ll amount to nothing and will change nobody’s life for the better. I would never bring anybody happiness, and would never remain a fond memory in someone’s life. Whether I lived or died wouldn’t matter, because nothing I do matters. I save nothing and no

one, and will eventually end in a grave so overgrown nobody even knows it was ever there.”

“Your future,” Mydei breathes, still unable to look at Phainon’s face, “is to deliver us. You will bring the new dawn. You’ll become the dawn, Deliverer.”

There’s a distant sound of chimes.

“May this world never again need a Deliverer,” he says, musing, as if someone said that to him before. “You know, when we were children, we’d draw cards to determine our future. People would get the knight card, or a princess, or just a hunter—but me, without fail, in every life, in every form, always; I would always draw the Deliverer card. I can’t be the Deliverer. How could I be the Deliverer? The Deliverer is a person worthy of love and trust, with no flaws or faults, and the only person that could fulfil Era Nova. So I’ll be the Deliverer. I’ll be the Deliverer. Look.”

Phainon procures a card from who-knows-where and he shows it to Mydei.

“Nothing,” he says, putting the card in Mydei’s hands, “nothing weighs heavier than this.”

Mydei has to steel himself, for the man tells no lie: this card is heavier than many things Mydei has lifted in his life. Looking up, he can finally glance at Phainon’s face and he gasps: he is cracked all over. A piece of his neck is missing, his left eye has crumbled away, and his skin looks like marble. This... isn’t what black tide corruption does to you, is it? Maybe Chrysos Heirs are different; maybe Phainon is different—

The chimes are getting louder.

“I didn’t tell anyone about it,” he says, “because by then, it was too late. I tried taking a bath while Castorice was away, but the water burned. I tried cutting it out, but even I dare not bleed myself dry. I had hoped that perhaps I am immune, or near it, and it would just—go away on its own, or at least, not get any worse. I didn’t want to worry Hyacine, because what could she do? Two weeks in, and I was sure it’d be fine. Of course, I felt terrible, but

that was a price I was willing to pay. My body burns, and I could feel it dissolve my insides. I didn’t want to die, but dying here isn’t so bad, is it?”

“You can’t stay,” Mydei whispers, still struggling to hold the card.

“I know,” that version of Phainon says, forlorn. “Can’t die before the end, right? I tried really hard, Mydei, I swear. Going home would’ve been nice. But I can’t see them again, right? Never again. In the new world... it doesn’t matter. You came all this way for me, didn’t you? Sorry about that. I could’ve found my own way out of here, if I were stronger, but I guess you know this place better, right? Haha...”

“Come back with me,” Mydei pleads. “Anaxagoras gave me a vial for your soul. With you inside, I can return to the living, and we can return your soul to your body—it’s not too late yet.”

“A vial, huh...” Phainon muses. “Alright. My soul—Phainon’s soul will be in that vial, as long as you take that card out with you. Don’t lose it, yeah? The card for the Deliverer... give it to its rightful owner, will you?”

The sound of chimes echoes directly in his ears now.

As Mydei blinks, Phainon is different—he wears the clothes of Khaos now. He stands amidst the burning fields of Aedes Elysiae. Mydei breathes.

“This, in your heart, will fade, Mydeimos,” he says and he doesn’t understand how he didn’t hear it before. “Losses are a constant on the flame-chase journey, and we never should have loved each other. Love will just make worse, always, in every life, and in every form. I will kill you, and your library is burned, as it has always been. The golden fields of Aedes Elysiae always burn, and we will destroy each other.”

Mydei feels himself getting weaker, indicating he’s waking up. He can see the flames clearly, but Phainon is fading away, and the houses in the distance have never existed. The swing has stopped forever, and nobody will ever sit on it ever again.

“Tell me what future the book holds in your mind, will you? Maybe if it were yours, one book would not be enough to record your future. I think... I just wanted—“

Mydei never hears the end of it, and the flames consume the withered golden fields until nothing is left.

*

Mydei wakes with a start, breathing hard. He sits up in a hurry, panting. His heart is beating too fast, and his eyes dart around. He’s in—a room. Not a battlefield. Good. That means he’s not in immediate danger.

“Impressive,” he hears a voice from off the side. “Both that woman and Castorice kept telling me you returning from the dead is not something they made up for fun. I would love to study you later. However, more pressing matters first: did you succeed?”

“Anaxagoras,” he breathes and blinks and the green-haired man.

“You even remember my name. Should I be honoured the savage royalty remembers me?”

Mydei frowns. He’s hardly savage. Hells, he’s hardly royalty. Aglaea is more royal than him.

“No,” he responds curtly and pulls out the vial. It is filled with a gentle golden glow. “Yes.”

Anaxagoras gets out of his chair and walks over, snatching the vial out of Mydei’s hand.

“Fascinating, truly fascinating.” His eye sparkles with excitement. “Why, if it weren’t so important, I would love to run some experiments with it. But I guess Phainon has given me enough already.”

“How long was I gone?”

“Shorter than expected,” Anaxagoras says, not looking at him. He holds the vial gently now, cupped in his palm like a fledging bird. “It has been barely more than a day. I sent Hyacine and Castorice off to sleep—they’ll be quite upset you chose to return now. Did you run into any trouble?”

“No, I,” Mydei stops-starts. He hesitates. There had been... something else, besides Phainon, hadn’t there? He can’t remember clearly. He shakes his head.

“Finding him was difficult at first, but I managed just fine. Now, the vial. How do we return the soul inside?”

Anaxagoras gets up and moves over to Phainon. He looks just like before, still as a doll and unmoving. Mydei hates it. Phainon isn’t even all quiet when he sleeps; he should never be this still. It’s not alright.

Anaxagoras straddles Phainon’s hips and Mydei frowns—is that a necessary step in the procedure? Anaxagoras holds the vial in his left hand, and he flexes his right for some reason. Suddenly, Mydei has a bad feeling about this.

“Who knows? The wonders of alchemy—you can’t bake a cake without breaking some eggs now, can you?!”

With that, he slightly tosses the vial in the air; and he smashes it on the way down.

“No, what are you doing?!”

As the fist makes contact with the vial and shatters it, a small golden explosion sounds and Anaxagoras gets blasted away against the next-best wall, while Mydei manages to shield his eyes from it. Checking quickly, he can assure that the man had not getting seriously hurt, so Mydei rushes over to Phainon.

His hands find the man’s shoulders, shaking him gently. For a moment, nothing happens, and then his eyelids flutter. Mydei’s heart skips a beat in relief. It worked, it really worked...!

“Deliverer,” he breathes and Phainon’s nose scrunches up. The man blinks and he looks up at Mydei with hazy eyes. His eyes are yellow, like the blazing sun, but after Mydei blinks, and Phainon blinks as well, his eyes are as blue as the sky again. Perhaps he imagined things.

“Mydei...?”

“Damn you, Deliverer,” Mydei cusses, “you got us all worried.”

“Ah... sorry...?”

Mydei smiles and leans down, pressing his forehead against Phainon.

“Don’t ever die before me again, Deliverer. I promised, didn’t I? If you die before me, I’ll kill you myself.”

“You... always did hold all your promises,” Phainon laughs quietly. His voice is weak and something tickles the back of Mydei’s head, but he can’t remember. Maybe it’ll come to him later. Phainon is back, and everything else can wait.

“I do,” he says, “and the two of us have a promise for tomorrow. I’m not letting you go, Deliverer. My Deliverer. Don’t ever go somewhere I cannot follow.”

“Okay,” Phainon agrees quietly, “until tomorrow and beyond, then.”

“Until tomorrow and beyond, then,” he says. “But tomorrow never comes.”

Before him lies Mydeimos, dead and slain, cut swiftly through his tenth thoracic vertebra, just like all the times before. Now, it doesn’t even matter if the prince shares his weakness, for he would only ever needed to have revealed it once, and yet, without fail, that weak-spot is always entrusted to Phainon.  Khaslana wonders if Mydeimos ever thought it would get used against him like this.

Before him lies Mydeimos, in a pool of his own blood, and the blood crowns his head in gold. The son of Gorgo will be crowned in blood, as it has always been. There is no other crown for Castrum Kremnos, and there never will be, because tomorrow is a lie. Tomorrow still sits among the distant stars, and Khaslana wonders how much longer it will be until the Deliverer comes.

“You never did say what the book said,” he muses, “and you never returned that card to me, either. Maybe the book never said anything, and you truly were holding the card for the Deliverer.”

Khaslana closes his eyes, and he doesn’t know if it’s in pain or not. He’s not the Deliverer, never has been, never could be, so... why? Why does it hurt thinking about someone agreeing with him about it? He’s just Khaslana, eternal Scourge of Amphoreus. Maybe the true Deliverer will pierce whatever is left of his heart, when they finally arrive.

“May you never remember the pain of death, Mydeimos,” he whispers, brushing golden hair out of his face. “All hail Mydeimos, the greatest conqueror, the mightiest protector, the strongest of them all. They dying lion, eyes blazing, the king with no kingdom.”

Selfishly, he leans down and presses his lips against a cooling forehead.

“May the Son of Gorgo be crowned in flowers.”

And as Khaslana leaves to stop Era Nova; to reset the cycle, to return to the ever-lasting yesterday; a singular blue flower blooms next to the head of the dead king, and its petals will flutter on the west wind once tomorrow comes.
